Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 42, verses 1–2:

These letters belong to the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) that occur at the beginnings of some surahs of the Noble Qur'an. We have already discussed them at more than one point, but we remind the reader that the Qur'an as a whole is built on connection (al-wasl): connection among its verses, connection among its surahs, and connection of its end with its beginning.

You read: ﴿مِنَ ٱلْجِنَّةِ وَٱلنَّاسِ﴾ [al-Nas: 6], "from among the jinn and mankind," with a kasra, so that you connect it to the basmala, "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," at the beginning of al-Fatiha. As for the disjointed letters, they are built on pausing (al-waqf), so that each letter is read separately. You say here (ha mim ayn sin qaf).

In the opening of al-Baqara you read (alif lam mim), and you read the same letters at the beginning of surah al-Sharh: ﴿أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ﴾ [al-Sharh: 1], "Did We not expand your breast for you?" so that you know that the Qur'an is not like any other book, and that its recitation depends first on hearing. The Exalted said: ﴿فَإِذَا قَرَأْنَاهُ فَٱتَّبِعْ قُرْآنَهُ * ثُمَّ إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا بَيَانَهُ﴾ [al-Qiyama: 18–19], "So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its explanation."

Therefore, when you contemplate the Qur'an, you find wisdom in reading with connection, and wisdom in reading with pausing. It is well known that the letter is the first building block in the construction of the word and, consequently, the phrase. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained to us the importance of pausing on these letters, and he said: The letters of language are of two kinds. Letters of structure (huruf mabna), which are the building blocks that enter into the construction of words and phrases. The word "kataba" (he wrote) is formed from the kaf, the ta' and the ba'. These letters give no meaning unless they combine with one another to form words. The other kind is letters of meaning (huruf ma'na), such as the kaf of comparison in "al-jundi ka-al-asad" (the soldier is like the lion). Here the kaf conveys the meaning of comparison, and these letters give no meaning unless they are combined with other words.

Language in general is a social phenomenon. It consists of expressions by which every people conveys its aims and by which they understand one another. As the scholars said, language is the daughter of imitation: what the ear hears, the tongue reproduces. A child who grows up in an Arab society speaks Arabic, and had he grown up in an English society he would have spoken English.

Therefore, language is neither a race nor a blood tie. It is a social phenomenon that depends on hearing. Even within a single language, you may hear a word for the first time and not understand it or know its meaning, although its words are Arabic, because they have never passed through your hearing before.

It is related that Abu 'Alqama the grammarian was infatuated with classical Arabic (al-fusha) and would speak only in it, bringing out strange words, until this troubled his servant, who did not understand many of these words. One night he woke from his sleep and asked the servant: "Ya ghulam, asqa'at al-'atarif?" The boy understood nothing except that he replied in distress and said to him: "Ziq faylam." Abu 'Alqama was surprised and said: "And what is ziq faylam?" The boy said: "And what is 'saqa'at al-'atarif'?" He said: "I meant: did the roosters crow?" He said: "And I meant: did they not crow?"

Among the curiosities of language: someone went to a physician, and the physician, whose name was A'yan, said to him: "What is wrong with you?" He said: "I ate some of the flesh of these jawaji', and I tasted a tasa'a from them, which caused me pain from al-wabila to the nape of the neck, and it kept growing until it mixed with al-halb, and the shara'if were hurt by it." The physician said: "Repeat it to me, for by God I did not understand anything from you." He repeated it as before. The physician replied and said to him: "Take harqafan, salqafan, sarqafan, zahzaqahu and zaqzaqahu with water of dung, then drink it." The man said: "Repeat it to me, for by God I did not understand anything from you." The physician said: "May God curse the least of us in making his companion understand."

Therefore, we say that language is the daughter of imitation. It depends first on hearing: what the ear hears, the tongue reproduces. A young child learns to speak from his family and from those around him, whereas the mute does not speak because he has not heard. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ [al-Baqara: 18], "Deaf, dumb, blind," for dumbness comes only after deafness. If we follow this question of how speech is learned back in its chain, we arrive at our father Adam (peace be upon him). Each of us learned speech from his father and mother and those around him, but Adam (peace be upon him) was taught by his Lord, as the Exalted said: ﴿وَعَلَّمَ ءَادَمَ ٱلأَسْمَآءَ كُلَّهَا﴾ [al-Baqara: 31], "And He taught Adam the names, all of them," meaning the names of things. God, glory be to Him, is the first Teacher.

In these disjointed letters there is an important lesson: they teach us faith in the unseen (al-iman bil-ghayb). How so? The Real, glory be to Him, has in His creation an unseen and a seen. God has given the unseen a seen that points to it. In the domain of beliefs, for example, I believe that this universe has a God who created it, and this belief can be demonstrated by the existing cosmic signs that are observed.

But in belief there also come unseen matters for which there is no proof from the perceptible seen, such as faith in the angels, who are unseen. And since there are obligations, obedience and disobedience, there must be a Paradise and a Fire, and before them the stage of the grave with what it contains of bliss or punishment. All these are matters known by transmission (sam'iyya) for which no rational proof is established. We believe in them because the God in whom we believe has informed us of their existence, and we trust His report.

Therefore, every observable article of belief carries alongside it an unseen faith. Faith in the unseen is the most important, because it is the touchstone of faith and the evidence of the strength of belief, since faith in the seen is shared by everyone.

Let us say: suppose you have a servant and you say to him: "O so-and-so, lift this stone in the garden, for example," and he says to you: "It is heavy, I cannot lift it." You say to him: "Under it is a purse of money from which I will give you your wages," and he hurries to it and lifts it. Is this faith in the unseen or in the seen? It is faith in the seen. He did not trust you; he trusted the purse of money.

Therefore, the true touchstone of faith is the unseen. For this reason the Exalted said, describing the believers: ﴿ٱلَّذِينَ يُؤْمِنُونَ بِٱلْغَيْبِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 3], "who believe in the unseen," because the sensed and the seen, everyone knows and believes in.

The same holds for the speech of the Lord of the Worlds and His Noble Qur'an: there is speech and letters that have a meaning, and other letters whose clear meaning we do not know or understand its interpretation. These are the disjointed letters, which we believe in and affirm as being from the unseen.

We have already clarified that the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs take up half the letters of the alphabet, that is, fourteen letters. Whoever contemplates these letters finds in them an order and a regularity that were not taken haphazardly. If we divide the letters of the alphabet into nine letters at the beginning, nine at the end, and ten remaining in the middle, we find that the disjointed letters took only two letters from the first group, namely alif and ha', and left seven; they took seven from the last group and left two; and from the middle they took the unpointed letters and left the pointed ones. Therefore, they have measures and wisdom.

We try and think about the meanings of these letters. The mind hovers around these meanings; it may reach some of them, or it may stand helpless, saying: "God knows best what He means." Every scholar who tries to understand these letters or to draw out the wisdom in them is a mujtahid and is rewarded, whether he hits the truth or misses it.

The essential point is that the Real, glory be to Him, wants us to believe in these letters and to accept them as they are, whether or not we know their meanings. They are like the teeth of a key: what matters to you is that it opens for you, without your knowing its mechanism, and it is enough that its owner knows its secrets and that it performs its task as it is.

It is true that we hover around these meanings and may reach something of them, but the Qur'an retains its inimitability (i'jaz), and these letters retain a renewed bounty that never runs out. When the Qur'an challenged the Arabs and rendered them incapable, some understood from this that it belittled the Arabs. But this challenge means their excellence in this domain and their mastery of it; otherwise the Qur'an would not have challenged them. Therefore, the Qur'an's challenge to them is an honour for them and an elevation of their standing, and it is enough that God made them the measure in this matter.

When the Qur'an challenged the Arabs, it did not bring new words or new letters. It is the same letters and the same materials of which their language is composed, yet the speech of the Real, glory be to Him, remained the inimitable, and they were unable to produce its like. The aspect of inimitability here is that the Qur'an is the speech of God: God is the One who speaks, so His speech is inimitable, because He, glory be to Him, bestows upon it of His power, whereas your speech, O servant, is not inimitable, because there is in it something of your incapacity.

Surat al-Shura is among the surahs of al-Hawamim, that is, the surahs that begin with the Exalted's words (ha mim). We have seen that these letters came as a single letter, such as (nun), (qaf) and (sad); as two letters, such as (ta sin); as three letters, such as (alif lam mim) and (ta sin mim); as four letters, such as (alif lam ra') and (alif lam sad); and as five letters, such as (ha mim ayn sin qaf) and (kaf ha ya ayn sad). The meanings of these letters are not known, and we believe that they are from the unseen which we must accept, and we say in their interpretation: God knows best what He means.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 42, verse 3:

﴿Thus does He reveal to you, and to those before you, Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾

The kaf in kadhalika (ذَلِكَ) is a particle of meaning that denotes comparison, and dhalika is a reference to the disjointed letters mentioned earlier. The meaning is: by means of such letters, He reveals to you and to those before you. These letters are therefore a revelation from Allah to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), and what follows them is likewise revelation from Allah.

Wahy (revelation, inspiration) is the communication of a hidden matter from the speaker to the hearer. For instance, if a guest comes to you and you wish to tell your servant something without the guest perceiving it, you look at the servant or whisper to him in a way that conveys what you mean. It is as though you had revealed that matter to him.

Wahy necessarily involves a revealer (mūḥī), a person to whom it is revealed (mūḥan ilayhi), and a thing revealed (mūḥan bihi). Allah, glory be to Him, has told us that He reveals to whomever He wills among His creatures. He reveals to the angels: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed..."﴾ [al-Anfal: 12].

He reveals to the messengers: ﴿Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him, and We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob...﴾ [an-Nisa: 163].

He reveals to His righteous servants, as He revealed to the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), and as He revealed to the mother of Moses, and He revealed to the ant, and He revealed to the earth, which is inanimate: ﴿Because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [az-Zalzalah: 5].

Likewise, Allah has told us that the devils reveal to one another, and so do the devils of mankind. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire to their allies...﴾ [al-An'am: 121], meaning from among mankind; and He said: ﴿They inspire one another with decorative speech in delusion﴾ [al-An'am: 112]. The general characteristic of the word wahy is that it is done in concealment. This is the general meaning of the word wahy, and it may be for good or for evil.

As for the legal (shar'i) revelation intended here, it is that which comes from Allah, the Exalted, to His Messenger (ﷺ) through the angel Gabriel (peace be upon him). He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills. Indeed, He is Most High, Most Wise﴾ [ash-Shura: 51].

Thus, legal revelation is Allah's communication to whomever He chooses among the messengers by one of these means: that He sends to him an angel, or by inspiration (ilham). We have already explained that the inspiration of the Merciful does not clash with the whisperings of Satan, because the inspiration of the Merciful is stronger and nothing contends with it.

In the story of the mother of Moses, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]. The wahy here means that He inspired her, or breathed into her heart, or set into her mind: ﴿Nurse him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river﴾. This is a command that reason would not accept, but because it came from Allah, no other choice opposed it, and the mother of Moses submitted to it and carried it out immediately.

Therefore, when Allah, the Exalted, wanted to teach the Companions of the Messenger of Allah the matters of their religion, He sent Gabriel to them in the form of a man, who began to ask the Messenger of Allah about faith, Islam and excellence (ihsan). He would ask and then affirm the answers, which surprised the Companions: how could he ask and then affirm? When the lesson ended, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That was Gabriel, who came to teach you the matters of your religion."

This verse shows that the one who reveals is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and it did not say, for example, "your Lord." It chose the word of divinity (uluhiyyah). Why? Allah is the One truly worthy of worship, and the one who is worshipped has a method and obligations, which include commands and prohibitions. The bestowal of divinity, as we have said, is a bestowal of obligation, whereas the bestowal of lordship is nurturing, care and provision without any return.

In both bestowals, the Exalted gains nothing from His servants and benefits from them in nothing. The obedience of the obedient does not benefit Him, and the disobedience of the disobedient does not harm Him. He made the obligation and the method only for the happiness of the servants and the wellbeing of society.

It is as though Allah were saying to us: "I want you to be happy in a clean, pure society, founded on love and peace, free of rancour, envy and hypocrisy, a society that enjoins and promotes virtue and is free of vice. That is because you are My servants and My creation, and every maker wants his creation to be sound and keeps it far from corruption."

Therefore we have said: the sensible man does not harbour resentment towards, or envy of, someone who is above him in some respect. When he encounters an oppressor, he does not curse him but prays for him. When he sees corruption, he sets it right. When he sees non-Muslims, he wishes that they were Muslims. Why? Because he will be made happy by their reform, will reap the fruits of their righteousness and uprightness, and their good will return to him.

As for His saying, ﴿Allah, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, it indicates that the One who reveals this revelation and sends down this Book and this method is (Allah), that is, the Lord of the obligations and the One who commands them.

Allah (اللَّه) is a proper name for the Necessarily Existent. Some have said it is derived from ilah, meaning worship, and ma'luh means worshipped. Others have said that Allah is a proper name for the Essence, and you find in it nothing but the quality of being a proper name for the Necessarily Existent. This name is described by all the attributes of perfection: He is the Strong, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Proud, the Merciful, the Wise, the Forgiving, the Bestower, the Subduer. These are among the names of the Exalted, and they are attributes of perfection of the name Allah. For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra: 110].

The Exalted teaches us how to call upon Him in all our affairs. Whoever seeks knowledge calls upon the All-Knowing; whoever seeks strength says, "O Strong, strengthen me"; whoever seeks wisdom says, "O Wise, inspire me with wisdom"; whoever seeks abundance of provision says, "O Provider, expand my provision for me." And if he wants all these attributes, he says, "O Allah." He is the name comprising all attributes of perfection.

He, glory be to Him, in His obligations to you is al-'Aziz (الْعَزِيزُ), meaning: the Victorious who cannot be overcome, possessing the attributes of might, majesty, wealth and self-sufficiency free from creation.

Then He, glory be to Him, is al-Hakim (الْحَكِيمُ), meaning: when He imposes obligations, He imposes them in measure and with wisdom. This is because the Qur'an contains obligations that some may see as burdensome. But if we take these obligations together with their fruit and the reward for them, we find them easy and light, because they yield for you a benefit before which all hardships become trivial.

Do you not see that you toil in this world and then gather fruit in proportion to your toil? Do you not see that the excellence of the result is in proportion to the effort? In this world, for example, you plant radishes and find radishes, and you can eat from them after a few days; you plant cucumbers and eat from them after forty days; rice after several months; and you plant a mango tree which gives you nothing until after several years.

Therefore, if Allah imposes on you something that involves hardship, know that the fruit is in proportion to it, and know that the One who revealed this obligation to the Prophet is Almighty and All-Wise. If it seems hard in your view, then the one who imposed it is free of you and of your obedience; He gains nothing from it, but you are the one who benefits. And He is All-Wise, meaning He imposed on you what leads to the soundness of your conduct in society.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 42, verse 4:

That is: to Allah, Exalted is He, belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, as absolute dominion, over which no vicegerent (khalifah) has any right of disposal. This is a forbidden zone: no one may dispose of a dominion that belongs to Allah alone. The vicegerent acts only within what lies below that, in the matters of events.

When we survey this verse and its like in the Qur'an, we find that the Truth, glorified is He, says once: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 4], and says once: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nahl: 52]. That is because creation varies. There is a creation that exists both in the heaven and on the earth, namely the angels; there is a creation only for the heaven, namely the exalted angels; and there is a creation only for the earth, namely the jinn and mankind.

So when He says: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 4], He mentions both kinds; and when He says: ﴿And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Nahl: 52], He mentions the kind they share.

From this we understand that the universe in which we live is not in truth the property of anyone. Ownership belongs to Allah, Exalted is He, and if He grants some ownership to a part of His creation, it is temporary. From the inner meaning of His dominion, lest the owners of property be deceived by their possessions: you are merely a vicegerent, not an owner. This earth is like a playground in which we all only play, and none of us owns it: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 120].

They have said: the lam (ل) is for ownership, as in: "the pen is for Zayd" (al-qalam li-Zayd). And it is for specification (ikhtisas), as when you say: "the rope is for the horse" (al-habl lil-faras). The horse does not own the rope; its owner does, but the rope is specific to the horse.

In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 4], both meanings are conveyed: it denotes ownership, and it denotes specification or restriction (qasr) through the fronting of the predicate, the prepositional phrase "lahu" (to Him). So dominion here belongs to Allah alone, and no one shares His dominion. You say "lizayd al-qalam" meaning the pen is specific to him and restricted to him, whereas in "al-qalam li-Zayd" you could say "and for 'Amr" as well.

The pronoun (ha') in "lahu" (to Him) refers back to the Truth, glorified is He. Absence here is itself manifestness and presence. And among His greatness, glorified is He, is that He is unseen and cannot be perceived by the senses: ﴿Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-An'am: 103].

Among His greatness is that He is unseen, just as we say: "al-haqq" (the truth), a word everyone claims for themselves, that they are upon the truth; and likewise justice. These are meanings we speak of, yet we do not know what they are. What is their form? So if we cannot even perceive pure lofty meanings, how can we hope to perceive the very essence of the Truth, glorified is He?

In another place He, glorified is He, said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 49]. So Allah owns the heavens and the earth, and they are a container in which there are things that also belong to Allah: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 4]. What is in the heaven is more precious than the heaven, and what is on the earth is more precious than the earth, for it is the custom that the contained is more precious than the container that holds it.

So everything in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Allah and is subjected to serve His vicegerent on His earth. The Truth, glorified is He, created for you before He created you, and prepared for you a universe ready to receive you, in which are the foundations of your life. This is what we said: it is the gift of lordship (ʿata' al-rububiyyah).

Your Lord nurtured you by the method He sent down from heaven through the hand of the messengers, and preserved for you the means of life and the sustaining of life by water that descends from heaven, and earth that brings forth for you various foods and sustenance, and He made for you rivers, and He made for you air.

Through these three elements the sustaining of your life is completed. We have said: among Allah's mercy toward His creatures is that your need for food is different from your need for drink, which is different from your need for breath. A person may endure without food for a month, for example, and endure without water for several days, but he cannot endure without air even for a single breath.

Therefore Allah made food the possession of some of mankind; if He withholds it from you, you live on the reserves in your body until you find a way to obtain it by any means. He made water scarce, because enduring its lack is less than enduring the lack of food. As for air, He did not make it the possession of anyone. Imagine that the owner of the air became angry with you: by Allah, you would die before you obtained his pleasure.

After that He gave you the luxuries of life and what you adorn and beautify yourself with. Therefore He said of the sea: ﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾ [al-Nahl: 14], and He said: ﴿O Children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to conceal your private parts, and as adornment (riyash)﴾ [al-A'raf: 26]. The necessary part of clothing is what covers the private parts, and then comes the adornment (al-riyash), which is what serves as decoration. ﴿And the garment of righteousness, that is best﴾ [al-A'raf: 26], because the garment of this world covers your nakedness and protects you in this world, whereas the garment of piety covers you in this world and in the Hereafter, and gives you another life that is more enduring and more lasting.

All of this is from the dominion of Allah that is on the earth. If you look upward, you find the air, which is a blessing containing many blessings within it, for air is an essential element in the continuation of life for living creatures, and it is the conducting medium through which sound and the images we see on the (television) are transmitted, for example.

Then reflect upon the heaven, with its sun, moon, stars, planets and galaxies: all are cosmic signs that belong to Allah, Exalted is He, and no one else disposes of them, glorified is He.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [al-Shura: 4]. "Al-'Ali" (the Most High) does not mean merely that He is high in place; rather, al-'Ali means the One exalted above everything in existence. ﴿Al-'Azim﴾ (the Most Great) likewise does not mean largeness of size; rather, al-'Azim is great in His self-subsistence (qayyumiyyah), His power, and His attributes of perfection.

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿تَكَادُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتُ..﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5] means: "The heavens are about to..." Ash-Sha'rawi says: "أي: تقترب وتوشك" means "that is, they draw near and are on the verge." ﴿يَتَفَطَّرْنَ﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5] means "split apart" or "are rent asunder." This is either from awe of God and His greatness, as the noble hadith reports: "..." and [the hadith text is incomplete in the source]. Or it is from anger at those who said, "God has taken a son."

﴿مِن فَوْقِهِنَّ..﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5] means "from above them." It may refer to the angels of the Higher Assembly (al-Mala' al-A'la), where the angels' awe of God and their exaltation of Him are found. Or it may refer to the earth, where are humankind, the sinners, and those who said, "God has taken a son." God answered them: ﴿You have certainly brought forth a thing, an abomination﴾ [Maryam: 89], meaning something strange and bizarre that the intellect does not accept. ﴿The heavens are about to be torn apart from it, and the earth split open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90].

A son is sought either for help in a time of weakness and old age, or for the perpetuation of one's remembrance. These are matters that are not permissible and not befitting for God, the Most High, because He is free of need of them. For this reason He, the Most High, said: ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92]. That is, if God, the Most High, had wished to take a son, He would have done so, since nothing prevents Him from it. Rather, the majesty, greatness, and self-subsistence of God, the Most High, do not allow for this. It is not permissible nor valid that He should have a son. The negation of appropriateness indicates perfection.

An example of this is His, the Most High's, saying about His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), when the disbelievers accused him of being a poet: ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾ [Ya-Sin: 69]. The meaning is that he does not speak poetry not because he is incapable of composing it. Rather, he possesses the tools of poetry and is able to do it, but it is not befitting for him to say it, and it is not proper, because God is preparing him for a matter greater than your poetry.

So His, the Most High's, saying ﴿It is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 92] is an affirmation that if He, the Most High, wished to have a son, He would have done so, but this is a matter that is not appropriate for Him, the Most High, because He is exalted above it. For this reason He said in another place: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 81]. That is, supposing He had taken a son, I would be the first of the believers in him.

And His saying: ﴿and the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5]. The angels belong to the unseen, while the heavens and earth belong to the perceptible. The perceptible things are angry, nearly splitting apart at this statement. As for the angels, they glorify their Lord with praise and declare Him free of having a son. Glorification (tasbih) comes before praise (tahmid). Tasbih means negating resemblance to any being whatsoever, while tahmid is due to God, the Most High, for His blessings and gifts. Therefore tasbih takes precedence over tahmid and is placed before it.

His, the Most High's, saying: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5]. They do not seek forgiveness for themselves but for those on the earth, which means they are without sins. Had they had sins, they would have sought forgiveness for themselves first. The seeking of forgiveness here is general for everyone on the earth, including the disbelievers.

In another place He said: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. Here He said: ﴿for those on the earth﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5], which encompasses all. Seeking forgiveness for non-believers means asking for their forgiveness and asking for their guidance, and that God inspire them with faith in Him.

As for the noble hadith in which it is reported: "They said: ..." [the hadith text is incomplete in the source]. The supplication here for the one who withholds (wealth) for ruin does not conflict with the angels' seeking forgiveness for those on the earth, because the one who spends detaches from his wealth and spends it in the way of God, so his love for God is greater than his love for wealth. As for the one who withholds, he loves his wealth and is stingy with it. When the angel supplicates against you for its ruin, he does so only to purify him from wealth that has diverted him from God. The ruin of this wealth is either a blessing or a calamity for which he is rewarded.

Thus: it is a supplication for good in both cases.

﴿Indeed, God is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5]. We have said that "alā" (indeed/listen) is a particle used to open speech and to alert the listener, because the speaker is free to speak whenever he wishes, but the listener is not free in hearing, and may neglect to hear some of the speech. Therefore the speaker should alert the listener and rouse him from his heedlessness, especially if the speech is important and he wants the listener to hear it without missing any of it. For this reason one says "alā" at the beginning, meaning: pay attention and listen to me.

Among examples of this is the saying of the pre-Islamic poet:

"Awake, and pour out in your cup for us, and do not leave the wines of Andarin."

The concluding phrase of the verse, ﴿Indeed, God is the All-Forgiving, the Most Merciful﴾ [Ash-Shura: 5], fits the matter of the angels' seeking forgiveness for those on the earth, and says to you: Pay attention, for the One whose forgiveness you seek is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. Al-Ghafur is the One who forgives sin and erases its traces, and Ar-Rahim means He shows mercy to you, so that you do not fall into another sin afterward.

Meaning of ﴿beside Him﴾ [al-Shura: 6], i.e., besides Allah, ﴿protectors﴾ whom they take as allies and worship besides Allah, like those who worshipped the sun and the moon, or the devils, or the angels. ﴿Allah is Watchful over them﴾ [al-Shura: 6], meaning: a Watcher who knows what they do, records what they say, calls them to account for it, and repays them with what they deserve, because to Him is the return and to Him is the final destination.

Since the matter is so, do not grieve, O Muhammad, and do not destroy yourself with regret over them. It is not upon you to guide them; upon you is only the conveyance (of the message). ﴿And you are not a guardian over them﴾ [al-Shura: 6]. Wakil (guardian): fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (passive), meaning: you are not entrusted with them so that they believe. Upon you is only the conveyance, and upon Us is the reckoning.

It is known that the pattern fa'il comes in the sense of fa'il (active), like rahim meaning rahim (merciful, one who shows mercy), and in the sense of maf'ul (passive), like qatil meaning maqtul (slain).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 42, verse 7:

The words "Thus" (kadhalika) mean: like this revelation that preceded, ﴿We have revealed to you an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. It is called "Qur'an" because it is recited (maqru'), and it is called "the Book" because it is written, inscribed in a book. It is described as "Arabic" because it is in letters and in a clear Arabic tongue, and "Arabic" is attributed to the Arabs. We have said that language is words through which every people expresses its purposes, and that it is the daughter of imitation: what the ear hears, the tongue reproduces.

Language is neither race nor blood, as evidence shows: if an Arab child grew up in a foreign environment, he would speak the same language as its people, because language is imitation and mimicry that depends on receiving and copying. Even in your own language, a word may occur to you whose meaning you do not know, and why? Because you never heard it before.

Therefore we say: teaching in language is evidence for the truthfulness of the Exalted One in what He said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. God, the Exalted, is the first teacher of mankind; otherwise, who taught Adam the names, the letters and the words?

Some orientalists stopped at this verse and said: how can the Qur'an be Arabic when it contains many words from other languages, from the language of the Romans, the Persians and the Abyssinians? We say: the meaning of ﴿an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [al-Shura: 7] is that it was revealed with words that circulated on the tongues of the Arabs and were passed among them before the Qur'an was revealed, so they became part of their language. Then, how many are these words compared to the words of the Qur'an?

Thus the Qur'an is Arabic, and God says: ﴿We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, to make [the message] clear to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 4], meaning: they receive from him and understand from him; otherwise the delivery of the message from God would not be complete.

If you say: how is that, when Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent to all people everywhere and at all times? We say: this is the task of the nation of Muhammad after him, to learn these languages and carry the religion of God to them wherever they are, because Muhammad is the Seal of the Messengers and the last of the Prophets, so the nation after him must bear this task and travel with it throughout the regions of the world.

The Qur'an was revealed in Arabic because He, glory be to Him, chose the Arabs to carry this message. We spoke earlier, in a nearby passage, about the choice of the Arabs in particular for this task, and the wisdom in the Messenger of God being unlettered among an unlettered nation. If the Qur'an is miraculous to the Arabs in its wording and style, it is miraculous to non-Arabs in its meaning, and miraculous in its cosmic signs that appear to people and astonish them from time to time.

Imagine that Muhammad had been educated among an educated people possessing a civilization: what would they have said, with the great number of disbelievers, opponents and atheists? By God, if that had been the case they would have said: Islam is a civilizational leap like those that occurred among many nations.

Therefore we say: illiteracy is a defect in every illiterate person, except in the Messenger of God, where it is an honour. Why? Because it means that he received all his knowledge and all his culture from the highest source, so it is an honour, owing to the elevation of its source to the Exalted One.

The strange thing is that among the enemies of Islam are those who say Muhammad was educated, though he is the one who wrote the Qur'an from his own self. Glory be to God! Are you more zealous for Muhammad than his own followers? The Qur'an is explicit in refuting them: ﴿You did not recite before it any book, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have had cause for doubt﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 48].

After this illiteracy, Muhammad (ﷺ) brought a method by which he subdued the civilizations of the world, and the two greatest civilizations of this era submitted to him: the civilization of Persia in the East and the civilization of Rome in the West. He subdued them not by force but by his methods and his lofty meanings, which organize the movement of life and of society as a whole, and cleanse it of all the filth and negative things that were widespread among them.

As for the words of God: ﴿that you may warn the Mother of Cities and those around it﴾ [al-Shura: 7]: warning (al-indhar) is informing of evil before its time and frightening with it before its appointed date. The wisdom is that when I frighten you of a matter before it happens, I give you the chance to avoid it.

﴿The Mother of Cities﴾ [al-Shura: 7] is Mecca; it is the mother of cities, or the origin of cities, because in it is the first house set for people, and Adam is among the people; so the House was set down before Adam. Therefore the saying that the angels were the ones who built this House is a sound opinion.

What is meant by "those around it" is the villages, tribes and Arab gatherings around Mecca. Because Mecca is the mother of cities and its origin, Quraysh took the leading position among the Arab tribes in the Arabian Peninsula. Quraysh had the honour of serving the House; they were its custodians who managed its affairs, and all the tribes came to them in the season of pilgrimage, so they were provided security, protection and sustenance. Therefore the trading caravans of Quraysh were given attention and protection throughout the regions of the Peninsula, on their winter and summer journeys.

So the House is what granted Quraysh this awe and this rank. God says: ﴿For the covenant of Quraysh, their covenant of the caravans of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 1-4]. Thus the lordship of Quraysh derives from the lordship of the House, from their neighbourhood to it and their standing in service to its pilgrims; had the House been destroyed, Quraysh's awe would have vanished and they would have lost this standing.

As for the words of God: ﴿and that you may warn of the Day of Gathering, about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Shura: 7]: that is, you frighten them of this day, which is the Day of Resurrection. The gathering on this day occurs in several respects: firstly, the Resurrection, in which body and spirit are joined; the angels in the highest assembly are gathered with humans; the oppressor and the oppressed are gathered, and the follower and the followed.

We note in this Qur'anic expression, ﴿and warn of the Day of Gathering﴾ [al-Shura: 7], that it is silent and does not mention the object of the verb (tundhira, "warn"), which takes two objects, as in His words: ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13]. Here the feared thing is mentioned in general, and the object of "warn" is not mentioned. Why? Because there will come another explanation for it. In His words, ﴿And warn them of the Approaching Day...﴾ [Ghafir: 18], that is, warn the disbelievers; this is the first object, and "the Day of Gathering" is the second object.

As for His words, ﴿about which there is no doubt﴾ [al-Shura: 7], meaning there is no uncertainty. ﴿A party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. For as long as there is obligation, there must be obedience and disobedience: the obedient is rewarded and the disobedient is punished. This is a custom even among people in the affairs of their lives, as is shown by their having made for it a law of reward and punishment. Likewise, on the Day of Gathering, about which there is no doubt, people will be in two divisions: a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.

In the language there is a style called (al-ihtibak), meaning "the well-woven matter," which is to omit from one thing what another mentions by way of contrast. Among it is His words: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two armies that met﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13], meaning a wondrous matter, ﴿in a battle﴾, meaning in war: ﴿one company fighting in the way of God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13], which is the believing company, ﴿and another disbelieving﴾ [Al 'Imran: 13], meaning fighting in the way of Satan.

Reflect on this Qur'anic structure and you will find that it omitted the attribute (believing) because His words ﴿fighting in the way of God﴾ indicate it; and for the other it mentioned the attribute (disbelieving) and omitted the contrast, that is, fighting in the way of Satan. Thus each omits from one what the other indicates by contrast; this is called ihtibak.

As for His words, ﴿a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7], it is a division after the gathering in His words ﴿and warn of the Day of Gathering﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. Division after gathering is another of the Qur'an's styles; there are gathering, division and classification.

Among it is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿On the day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission﴾ [Hud: 105]: this is gathering. ﴿Among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105]: this is division. Then He classifies and details what is said about each party: ﴿As for those who were wretched, they will be in the Fire, having therein groaning and wailing, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills; indeed your Lord is the Accomplisher of what He intends. And as for those who were made happy, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills, a gift uninterrupted﴾ [Hud: 106-108].

But why this division, ﴿a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]? They said: because the Exalted One created creation and gave them choice when He offered them the trust, which is the trust of obligation, in His words: ﴿We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it; indeed he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72].

That is: We left them free choice to bear the trust, so every created thing feared to bear it and chose to be subjected, its Lord disposing of it as He wills, except humans and jinn, who chose to bear the trust. ﴿Indeed he was a wrongdoer﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72], that is, to himself; ﴿ignorant﴾ of the consequences, because you guarantee yourself at the moment of undertaking, but you do not guarantee the moment of fulfilment; your circumstances may come between you and the discharge of the trust. Because man chose to bear the trust and chose choice, he had to be called to account for his trust, whether he preserved it or squandered it, and he had to have an abode of recompense and reckoning: a party in the Garden and a party in the Blaze.

Commentary: al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66), on surah 42, verse 8:

That is: do not be astonished at the command of Allah. He has absolute will over His creation. Had His will been a will of compulsion, no one could have gone out against it, and all of mankind would have been believers. But there is a difference between faith through compulsion and coercion, and faith through love and choice.

Exalted is He, does not desire from us mere rigid shells; rather He desires loving hearts. He desires them willingly and by choice. We have previously given an example of this, and to God belongs the highest example: a man who has two slaves, one of them free and unrestrained, the other tied to his master by a rope. When the master calls, both come and answer his call. Which of them is more obedient, and which of them loves him?

When Allah, exalted is He, offered the trust (al-amanah) to all creation and gave them the choice, He established both aspects: compulsion and power, and He established love. He established power and compulsion in that He made a category of His creation, namely the heavens, the earth and all existing things other than humans and jinn, come obediently and in faith, and surrender their choice to the choice of their Lord and Creator. Then He established love in the choice of humans and jinn, because they believed out of love while they were able to disbelieve.

﴿But He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Shura: 8]. These are the believers, who are admitted into Paradise by Allah's bounty and mercy, not by their deeds; deeds are a means of entering Paradise. On the other hand, ﴿and the wrongdoers, they have no protector nor helper﴾ [al-Shura: 8]. That is: they will enter the Fire, because the group that entered Paradise entered it by Allah's bounty and mercy, while these are wrongdoers, and the recompense for wrongdoing is the Fire.

﴿They have no protector﴾ [al-Shura: 8]: a relative who would befriend them and ward off harm from them. ﴿Nor a helper﴾ [al-Shura: 8]: one who would support them even from afar, who sees them defeated and so is moved with compassion and supports them.

Then Exalted is He explained the cause of this, that they turned away from worshipping the One, the Unique, and took protectors besides Him, so they deserved this abandonment:

﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him? But Allah, He is the Protector...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 42, verse 9:

After Allah, glorified and exalted is He, established that the wrongdoers have no protector (wali) and no helper (nasir), this question follows: ﴿Or have they taken protectors besides Him?﴾ [al-Shura: 9] Do they have protectors we do not know of? The interrogative here is for negation and denial. Since they have no protectors, why did they not take Me as their protector? Or the meaning is: rather, they have taken protectors besides Him, and they should reflect on this and examine themselves.

﴿So Allah is the Protector﴾ [al-Shura: 9], the true Protector of whoever wills a protector and helper, ﴿and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things capable﴾ [al-Shura: 9]. He came here with two attributes that none of their protectors can possess: giving life to the dead and power. These attributes that are specific to Him, glorified is He, are found in the Qur'an always accompanied by the separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) to emphasize that they belong to Allah alone, and no one shares them with Him. Therefore He said: ﴿So Allah is the Protector, and He gives life to the dead, and He is over all things capable﴾ [al-Shura: 9].

And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And that it is He who causes laughter and causes weeping * And that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾ [al-Najm: 43-44]. These are actions that none can do except Allah alone. The meaning of "He causes laughter and weeping" is that He created in you the instinct of laughter and the instinct of weeping, as evidence by their existence in every son of Adam and in all nationalities. Laughter is one among the Arabs, the Indian, and the Russian, and likewise weeping. Therefore it is an instinct. Similarly, the matter of life and death belongs to Allah alone; none other than Him can do it.

In the story of our master Ibrahim, when he enumerated Allah's blessings upon him, he said: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me * And who feeds me and gives me drink * And when I am ill, it is He who cures me * And who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78-81].

In matters where there is a semblance of an action by someone other than Allah, He brings the separating pronoun (huwa) to emphasize that the action belongs to Allah alone, as in ﴿it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78], because guidance may come through the hand of one of the humans. And in ﴿who feeds me and gives me drink﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 79], a father, for example, may be thought to be the one who feeds me and gives me drink. Likewise in ﴿cures me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 80], because some may think the physician holds healing in his hand. But in the actions where there is no semblance of anyone's intervention, He brings them without emphasis, because they are purely for Allah, exalted is He, with no contender: ﴿and who causes me to die and then gives me life﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 81].

The giving of life to the dead is meant to refer to the resurrection in the Hereafter, and we have seen an example of it in this world, such as the story of ʿUzayr that the Qur'an relates: ﴿Or like one who passed by a town while it was fallen upon its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled. And look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh." And when it became clear to him, he said, "I know that Allah is over all things capable."﴾ [al-Baqara: 259].

That is because the sense of time comes from events; when events cease, the sense of time ceases. Therefore, when ʿUzayr had been dead for a hundred years, he said when Allah revived him: "I have remained a day or part of a day." So Allah, glorified is He, wanted to establish his truthfulness regarding the day or part of a day by his looking at his food, which he had with him, where he found it as it was, unchanged and not spoiled. And He wanted to establish the truthfulness of Allah, glorified is He, regarding the hundred years. So He said to him: look at your donkey and how it has become decayed bones, and this does not happen except over a hundred years.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and He is over all things capable﴾ [al-Shura: 9] indicates the absoluteness of Allah's power, exalted is He. This power is witnessed in His cosmic signs in the heavens, on the earth, and in the souls; all of them testify to Allah's absolute power.

Yes, Allah is over all things capable, and He has shown us examples of giving life to the dead in this world so that we may take from them proof of His truthfulness in giving life to the dead in the Hereafter. The story of ʿUzayr, whom Allah caused to die for a hundred years, has passed us by.

Another example is in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? Allah said to them, "Die," then He gave them life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward the people, but most of the people do not give thanks.﴾ [al-Baqara: 243].

Among the greatness of Allah, glorified is He, and His power over all things, is that He extends to His creation some of His power, so that He makes, for example, our master Ibrahim capable of giving life to the dead by Allah's permission. The strong among the humans, for example, when he sees a weak person, helps him and extends to him the effect of his strength, carrying his belongings for him, and the weak person remains weak.

As for Allah, glorified is He, when He extends His power to His servant, He makes him act by himself and transmits to him some of His power and some of His attributes, so the strength becomes intrinsic in you. You know the story of our master Ibrahim when he wanted to see the process of giving life to the dead with his own eyes, so he asked his Lord for that: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.' He said, 'Have you not believed?' He said, 'Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest.'﴾ [al-Baqara: 260].

That is: O Lord, I am a believer and I affirm, but I want assurance; I want to ascend to a higher rank of faith. Some orientalists, commenting on this verse, say: is faith other than the tranquility of the heart? And since he asked for the tranquility of the heart, then faith is deficient.

We say: Our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did not say, "Lord, will You give life to the dead or not?" Rather he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqara: 260]. He believes in Allah's giving life to the dead and affirms Allah's power over that, and he wants to know the how. So the assurance is regarding the modality, not the establishing of the attribute for Allah, exalted is He. It is like if I said to you, "How did you build this mosque?" Do I doubt its construction? No, it already exists, but I want to know the how.

Therefore Allah, glorified is He, responded to His prophet Ibrahim with a logical reply, for the modality of giving life to the dead is not known by speech but by action and practice. So He made him perform this act himself, practise the process of giving life to the dead and witness it: ﴿He said, "Then take four birds and incline them toward yourself"﴾ [al-Baqara: 260], meaning: make sure of them and of their marks, then slaughter them. ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them, then call them...﴾ [al-Baqara: 260]. So: you are the one who acts yourself, and this is from the greatness of the Creator, glorified is He.

So: ﴿and He gives life to the dead﴾ [al-Shura: 9] means: it is a process restricted to Him, glorified is He, even if He extends it to whomever of His servants He wills; He is its owner. ﴿And He is over all things capable﴾ [al-Shura: 9]. You find some creatures have power, as in some humans, for example, or some angels whom they took besides Allah, but their power is limited: if the angels are capable of doing one thing, they are incapable of other things. As for Allah, glorified is He, His power is absolute, nothing overcomes it; complete power over all things.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 42, verse 10:

Ikhtilaf (difference of opinion) is the failure of views to converge on a matter. The group divides into two or more sides, each supporting its own opinion and opposing the other's, and its opposite is wifaq (agreement). Opinions differ either in serious, fruitful discussion aimed at reaching the truth, or in contentious argument (jadal) and obstinacy (lajajah) that yields no benefit and is disputation over falsehood (mira' bil-batil).

Therefore, the Truthful (al-Haqq) subhanahu teaches us what to do when we differ: to refer the matter and the judgment to Allah. For example, when they differed over the soul (ruh) and asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿They ask you about the soul. Say: The soul is by the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ [al-Isra: 85].

Likewise, al-Haqq subhanahu taught us the etiquette of disagreement: not to rush to judgment, and to examine it objectively. The disputants may in reality be in agreement while not knowing the nature of that agreement. An example: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded the Companions, as they were heading towards Banu Qurayzah, that none should pray 'asr except in Banu Qurayzah. The time of maghrib came upon them while they were on the road, so they differed about the 'asr prayer. One group said: we must pray it now, before its time passes; another group said: No, rather we pray it in Banu Qurayzah as the Messenger of Allah commanded.

So: one opinion was zealous for the time, and another was zealous for the place. Whoever was zealous for the time prayed on the road, and whoever was zealous for the place prayed in Banu Qurayzah. When they met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they presented this disagreement to him, and he approved each of them in his opinion, and rebuked neither this one nor that one.

So: it was a superficial disagreement, while they did not realize that they were all upon the truth and in agreement. Thus, when we differ, we must refer the matter to Allah and to His Messenger, and be objective without zealotry. This concerns disagreement among believers.

Likewise, if the disagreement is with the People of the Book, Jews or Christians, refer your disagreement with them to Allah, because they have heavenly scriptures: the Torah and the Gospel, which contain attestation to Muhammad, the seal of the messengers, glad tidings of him, and his attributes and signs. The proof is that some of them believed after the mission of the Messenger of Allah. So refer your disagreement with them to Allah, so that you cut off from them the path of contention, obstinacy and enmity.

The meaning of ﴿So its judgment is with Allah﴾ [ash-Shura: 10] is also: and to the Messenger of Allah, because he is the deputy of Allah in rulings, and Allah has given him the right of legislation (tashri'), as evidenced by the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. This is a distinction that none of the messengers before the Messenger of Allah attained, for they were only charged with conveying (al-balagh), whereas our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was entrusted by his Lord with legislation. Therefore, when one of the disputants said: What is the evidence that Subh is two rak'ahs, Zuhr four, and Maghrib three? He replied: The evidence is the Exalted's saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr: 7].

Your referring the judgment in a disputed matter to the Truthful subhanahu, and presenting it to the word of Allah and the word of His Messenger, this return ends the disagreement and ends contention. No one is diminished by submitting to a higher authority upon which hearts converge in purity and contentment with His judgment, the Exalted. Do you not see that if the judgment against you comes from a human like yourself, you may not accept it even if it is correct? But when the judgment is Allah's, there is no reluctance and no embarrassment.

﴿That is Allah, my Lord; upon Him I have relied﴾ [ash-Shura: 10]. ﴿That﴾ (dhalikum) is a demonstrative for exaltation: dha is the indicator, the lam is for distance, and the kaf is for address. ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾: you say it while proud of it, exulting in your attribution to Him subhanahu, as if He were something lofty beyond every conception. And the Rabb, as we have said, is the One who undertakes nurturing (tarbiyah) and giving, from Whom comes grace and bounty; and upon Him I rely in all my affairs. ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾ [ash-Shura: 10]: I return and come back in the Hereafter for reckoning and recompense.

When I say ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾ [ash-Shura: 10], I am proud of the lordship (rububiyyah) that nurtures and gives, and proud of the divinity (uluhiyyah) that imposes obligations, because imposing obligations is part of complete nurturing. The requirement of my nurturing is that my worldly life be happy, but the world is time-limited and finite; true nurturing, then, is that I nurture you for something more enduring and lasting, namely the Hereafter, whose bliss never ends, and which I do not leave by death nor which leaves me by perishing.

Some say: the nurturing here is for the material. We say: for the material and also for values and the soul. Therefore the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾ [al-Anfal: 24]. What is the meaning of (yuhyikum, "gives you life") here? Did He not address them while they were living and hearing? Therefore the intended meaning is another life other than the life of matter; the intended meaning is the life of values and the soul, the eternal life that neither escapes you nor you it.

Therefore the curriculum that grants you this life is called a spirit (ruh). The Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit (ruhan) of Our command﴾ [ash-Shura: 52]: yes, a spirit, which gives you eternal life, whereas the first spirit gives you only the life of this world. The angel who descends with the curriculum is also called a spirit: ﴿The trustworthy Spirit (ar-Ruh al-Amin) has descended with it﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 193].

So we understand that the life required is not the life of this world; rather, the world is a means and an instrument conveying to a better end than it, and in order to reach this end, I must be upright upon the curriculum of the One who will give me this life.

Thus, ﴿That is Allah, my Lord﴾ [ash-Shura: 10] combined the term divinity (uluhiyyah), worship and obligation with the term lordship (rububiyyah), which nurtures, gives and bestows.

Contemplate the Qur'an's expression in the matter of reliance (tawakkul): ﴿upon Him I have relied﴾ ('alayhi tawakkaltu). The linguists call this style qasr (restriction) by fronting the prepositional phrase ('alayhi) before the verb (tawakkaltu), and this conveys restriction and exclusivity: my reliance is upon Allah and not upon other than Him. Whereas if you say: "I relied upon Allah," it is permissible to add: "and upon so-and-so." So the restrictive style confines reliance to Allah alone.

They said: reliance upon Allah is the resource of one who has lost the means and has left his own strength and power for the power of his Lord and Creator; for Allah the Exalted placed causes for everything, so when causes are scarce we resort to the Causer, subhanahu: ﴿Who answers the distressed one when he calls upon Him?﴾ [an-Naml: 62].

The mudtarr (distressed one) is one who has exhausted all available causes. At that point he does not surrender himself to events nor despair; rather, he says: I have a Lord above causes, who is their Creator and Causer, and He will not abandon me when I resort to Him.

We have previously mentioned to you the story of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) when Pharaoh and his soldiers overtook them and besieged them at the shore of the sea, until the companions of Musa said: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 61]. The reality of events was that the sea was before them and the enemy behind them, with no escape. But Musa had other calculations with his Lord, so he replied to them: ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 62].

This is the reliance that rests on trust in Allah, the reliance of the distressed one whose causes have become scarce and who has nothing left but to resort to Allah. Therefore the answer came from al-Haqq subhanahu as a timeless, dazzling miracle: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it parted, and each part was like a great mountain. And We brought near there the others. And We saved Musa and those with him, all together. Then We drowned the others﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 63-66].

Similarly, in ﴿And to Him I turn in repentance﴾ [ash-Shura: 10], there is a restrictive style by fronting the prepositional phrase before the verb, meaning: I return to Him alone, not to anyone else. And you notice in this style that reliance came in the past tense ﴿upon Him I have relied﴾ [ash-Shura: 10], whereas repentance came in the present tense ﴿And to Him I turn﴾ [ash-Shura: 10]. This precision of expression is because the speaker of these words is Allah.

It is natural to find this linguistic craftsmanship and precision, because reliance is a firmly established belief from the outset, even before you speak of it: it originates first and exists. Turning back to Him and returning, however, happens at the time of the event, in the future, when we return to Him subhanahu.

Then he speaks of another aspect of His power, and that He is the true Protector (al-Wali):

﴿Fatir as-samawati wal-ard, ja'ala lakum...﴾.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 42, verse 11

Then he speaks of another aspect of His power, and that He alone is the true Protector (al-Wali): "Originator of the heavens and the earth. He has made for you, from yourselves, mates..."

The Almighty said at the beginning of surah Fatir: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1]. The Fatir (the Originator) is the Creator who brings a thing into being without any prior pattern or model to follow, as happens, for example, in the world of industry today. There is an industrially advanced country, and countries less advanced than it come and take its industries, imitate them, and manufacture on its pattern. Of course, they develop, renew and add to them, but the first country retains precedence in the original model.

So the meaning of ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ is: their Creator and Innovator, who originated them without any prior pattern. ﴿He has made for you﴾ indicates that all things are created for the service of the children of Adam, this vicegerent (khalifah) whom Allah appointed over the universe...

As for His saying, ﴿He has made for you, from yourselves, mates﴾: by "mates" (azwaj) is meant here the male and the female, as in His saying: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs, of what the earth produces and of themselves and of what they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36].

This is a fact which modern science has established: pairing exists in everything, even in inanimate objects. We have understood it in the positive and negative in electricity, and we have seen it in the particles of matter. In earlier times they knew it in living things, in humans, animals and plants, and with scientific progress we have found it in everything God created.

This is the proof of the truth of His saying: ﴿and of what they do not know﴾ [Ya-Sin: 36]...

The meaning of ﴿from yourselves, mates﴾ is: from the same species and the same kind as you. Nature draws each of the two sexes, male and female, toward the other, so a mutual companionship arises between them, from which arises the instinct of sex, which is accompanied by pleasure. From the meeting of male and female offspring results. Thus, a human takes it both for offspring and for pleasure, whereas the animal takes it for offspring only: you see the male drawn to the female until conception occurs, after which he no longer approaches her.

As for the human, it is otherwise: the human takes it for pleasure, and then accuses the animal and says, "Bestial desire," when in reality it is human desire. So why do we wrong the beasts?

Among His blessings upon His creatures is that He made the mates of one kind, so that compatibility and harmony might be achieved between the two sexes, and procreation and the survival of the species might occur...

﴿And of the livestock, pairs﴾ was mentioned earlier in surah al-An'am: ﴿eight pairs: of the sheep two, and of the goats two. Say: Has He forbidden the two males or the two females, or that which the wombs of the two females contain? Inform me with knowledge, if you should be truthful. And of the camels two, and of the cattle two...﴾ [al-An'am: 143-144].

So: since He told us "eight pairs," then enumerated four, each kind consists of two pairs: a male and a female. ﴿He multiplies you by it﴾, that is, by the making (al-ja'l), i.e., He increases you. We note that He did not say "He multiplies you through it"; rather He said ﴿yadhra'ukum fihi﴾, and "fi" comes to mean "by means of it"...

As for His saying: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, it has its own relevance here. When the True, glorified is He, spoke of pairs in everything, He wished to declare His Essence exalted above this matter, so He said ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. To deny likeness we say, "Nothing is like him," but here He said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾.

So: He has made for Himself a likeness, because the Arabs speak of "the like" (al-mithl) and mean the person himself. If something happens from a person, they say to him, "One like you does not do this," meaning: you should not do it, because one like you does not do it, one like you does not flinch in war. But why do they not say, "You do not flinch in war," and instead use the like?

Consider the linguistic gradation here: when you say, "Zayd is like the lion," this means he is below the lion, since you have likened him to the superior in the quality. So: the like is less than the original. Were it supposed that the Truth had a like, we would not say that Allah has a like, because His like would be lower than Him. Thus He has no like, and this is the meaning of the poet's words:

"I did not say 'like you,' meaning by it other than You, O One without any likened."

So the style here in negating likeness is that He says "nothing is like Him." Rather, He wished to affirm this matter: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, meaning: even if there were a likeness to Allah, it would have no resemblance, so how much more so Allah, the Exalted? The word "thing" (shay') is applied to the genus of genera, meaning: everything that is called a thing, everything to which the term "thing" applies, has no likeness to Him.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾: here He mentioned two attributes shared between the True, glorified is He, and His creation. You hear and Allah hears, you see and Allah sees, but we must take these attributes of Allah within the frame of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, so hearing is not like hearing and sight is not like sight.

The meaning of "All-Hearing" is: of sounds; "All-Seeing": of visible things.

In another place He says, glorified is He: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71]. Hearing itself is an action, speech is an action, and sight is an action. We have previously clarified that action is speech and deed, speech being specific to the tongue, and deed encompassing the action of all the limbs apart from the tongue. Thus the tongue alone has taken a share of action, for speech carries the message, by it faith is declared, and by it a person expresses himself.

And this verse, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾, teaches us how to exalt Allah above every like, equal or counterpart, and teaches us to take every attribute shared between the Truth and creation within this framework of faith.

First, notice here the style of restriction (qasr) in ﴿To Him belong the keys of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 12], through the fronting of the prepositional phrase. So the keys of the heavens and the earth belong to Him alone, are His alone, and are restricted to Him, glorified is He; none shares them with Him.

The word ﴿maqalid﴾ [al-Shura: 12] is the plural of miqlad, which means the key (miftah). Therefore, He, the Exalted, said elsewhere: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He...﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. So to Him, glorified is He, belong the keys of good in the heavens and the earth. The meaning of "keys" is that they lock up something beneficial and useful.

The unseen (al-ghayb) is a treasury among these locked treasuries. When God gives the key of it to someone and informs him of some of the unseen, which He causes to flow upon his tongue, this is an act of honour and favour from Him, exalted is He, toward him. This does not mean that he has become a knower of the unseen and opened an office for the knowledge of the unseen. Rather, he takes his need, with which God has honoured him, and hands the key back to its owner: ﴿With Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He...﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. Whoever claims knowledge of the unseen does not know how to show proper courtesy toward God.

We use this word (maqalid) in our common language now, saying: so-and-so holds in his hand the maqalid of rule (al-hukm), or the maqalid of affairs in the company or the factory, meaning: he is the official who possesses the decision and holds in his hand the keys of the work and its secrets.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He expands the provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]...﴾ [al-Shura: 12], that is: here, by a key and a miqlad from these maqalid, which is the key of provision, He, glorified is He, expands it for whom He wills, widens it and eases it, and likewise He withholds it and constricts it upon whom He wills of His servants. The maqalid over provisions explain to us His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21], meaning: the expansion or constriction of provision is by knowledge, by measure, and by wisdom.

Do not think that provisions are distributed haphazardly, no. For the Distributor of them is All-Knowing of His creation and All-Aware of their secrets and hidden matters, Wise, who places each thing in its proper place. Therefore, do not be surprised when you see the wealthy, luxurious man who owns millions while his neighbour cannot find his daily sustenance. Do not be surprised when you see, for example, the owners of shops: this one buys and sells and has abundant provision, while beside him is a similar shop that no one enters. Do not be surprised, for behind this and that is a wisdom that whoever knows it has known, and whoever is ignorant of it has remained ignorant.

It is sufficient for you to read: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21], and here He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is All-Knowing of everything﴾ [al-Shura: 12], He knows who gives and who withholds. For this reason our master, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while clarifying these wisdoms for us, said: God, Mighty and Majestic, said in the hadith qudsi: And the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Nay! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-Alaq: 6-7].

So the poverty of the poor is for a wisdom, and the richness of the rich is for a wisdom. So do not object; reflect, for perhaps wealth in your hand is a tool of plunder, oppression, aggression and tyranny, and perhaps wealth calls you to disobedience or generates in you an inclination to evil. When God withholds this tool from you, He has withheld it only to show you mercy by poverty; richness does not suit you, and your righteousness lies in poverty, and in some contentment with what God has apportioned to you, and in not stretching your eyes toward one above you in the enjoyment and adornment of this world.

We often see the children of the rich corrupt because of the abundance of money in their hands, while you find the son of the poor safe from this, and perhaps in better condition than the son of the rich, and in our reality there are many examples of this.

The believer is required to live within the bounds of his material means. What wearies people now is that you find one of us imposing on himself a certain standard of living before imposing on himself an income that matches the standard he has chosen for himself. Then when shortfall occurs, he is compelled to the unlawful: to fraud, to theft, to bribery, and other means of unlawful gain to cover the expenses of his living.

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Let the one of wide means spend from his wide means, and whoever has his provision restricted, let him spend from what God has given him. God does not burden a soul except with what He has given it. God will bring about, after hardship, ease﴾ [al-Talaq: 7].

The believer enters the market and finds in it what is delicious and good: the Roumi (cheese), meats, fish and fruit. His soul may long for them, but he adorns himself with contentment and is satisfied with what is within his capacity, so he buys a kilo of green fava beans and half a kilo of cheese, and goes to eat in the midst of his children, and finds in this simple meal a taste and a pleasure that the rich man perhaps does not find.

But if his eye stretches to what is above his level, you see him buying on credit and eating as the rich eat, and perhaps he extravagantly wastes upon himself and enters the realm of squandering. Then after some days, there comes one who knocks on his door demanding his debt, and he finds from the humiliation of the demand more than what he found of the pleasure of the food.

Therefore, the Truth, glorified is He, addresses the son of Adam: "O son of Adam, I created you for worship, so do not play; and I have apportioned your provision, so do not exhaust yourself — and the exhaustion here does not mean the exhaustion of the limbs, but the exhaustion of thought, worry and preoccupation of the mind — so if you are content with what I have apportioned to you, I will ease your heart and body, and you will be praiseworthy with Me; and if you do not content yourself with what I have apportioned to you, then by My might and majesty, I will set the world upon you, you will run in it like the running of the wild beast in the wilderness, and then you will obtain from it only what I have apportioned to you, and you will be blameworthy with Me. O son of Adam, I created the heavens and the earth and I did not tire of creating them; would a loaf that I drive to you weary Me? O son of Adam, do not ask Me for tomorrow's provision, just as I do not ask you for tomorrow's work. O son of Adam, I love you, so by My right over you, love Me."

When the poor man is content with what God has apportioned to him, and does not aspire to what is above his level, God says to him: You were content with My decree, so now I give you according to your measure. Therefore you find all the great men of the world and its leaders began their lives in want and utter poverty, and they have told us about the history of some of these, and how they came from the bottom of society.

When you reflect on the matter of constricting provision for some of creation, you find in it a social wisdom: this disparity leads to a kind of complementarity among the elements of society. Imagine that the whole society were rich, with provision spread out for them all: who would then serve them?

Who would produce for them, cultivate, and attend to the lowest needs? Thus there must be a class of the poor to carry out this role, not out of mere favour, but out of need: the worker needs his wage so he works, and the servant needs his wage so he serves, sweeps and cleans. Need and benefit are what bind the elements of society together.

Strangely, you now see businessmen and those with interests complaining about workers: the worker says, as long as he has money and his pocket is full, he does not work until what he has of money runs out, then he returns to work, and so on.

I recall, among the anecdotes of our teacher, Shaykh Musa Sharif, may God have mercy on him, that once he said: "O God, provide for the scholars and make them rich, and keep the craftsmen poor." When we asked him, he said: because if the scholar is not rich, a fatwa may humiliate him; as for the craftsman or worker, he does not work except when he is in need of money.
